subject: Science
title: Properties of Matter
source: Mrs. Powell's 2nd Grade Math/Science slides (Properties of Matter Review, Bartholomew and the Oobleck, Oobleck), Non-Newtonian Flow experiment, Properties & Uses of Matter lessons 1–3
notes: The PDF doesn't say when the Properties of Matter quiz is — set the date under Grown-ups → Tests.
The Bartholomew and the Oobleck slides are mostly pictures, so only the oobleck experiment facts are included.

lesson.title: Three states
lesson.html:
Solid: its own shape and size (wood, glass, clay, metal, concrete).
Liquid: takes the shape of its container; has a definite volume.
Gas: no shape; fills its container.

lesson.title: Best for the job
lesson.html: We test materials for water resistance, absorbency, flexibility and strength, then match each material to the job using evidence: “Foil is best for blocking water because it stayed dry.”

lesson.title: Reversible or not?
lesson.html: Ice, chocolate and playdough can change back (reversible). Toasted bread cannot (irreversible). Changes: melting, freezing, cooking, breaking, mixing.

lesson.title: Oobleck
lesson.html: Cornstarch + water is a non-Newtonian fluid: slow touch = liquid, fast punch = solid.

list.q: What is a solid?
list.a: Matter that has its own shape and size
w: Matter that takes the shape of its container
Matter that fills a container and has no shape
list.why: A solid keeps its own shape and size.
list.hint: Think: does it stay the same shape?

list.q: What is a liquid?
list.a: Matter that does not have its own shape and takes the shape of its container
list.why: Liquids take the shape of their containers and have a definite volume.

list.q: Which is true about liquids?
w: They always stay in one place
list.why: A liquid has a definite volume (an amount).

list.q: What is a gas?
list.a: Matter with no shape that fills the container it is in
w: Matter that takes the container's shape but has a set volume
list.why: Gases do not have shape and fill their container.

list.q: Which of these is a solid?
list.why: Solids can be wood, glass, clay, metal or concrete.

list.q: Which of these is a solid?
list.why: Glass is a solid.

list.q: Which of these is a solid?
list.why: Metal is a solid.

list.q: Which of these is a solid?
list.why: Concrete is a solid.

list.q: Which of these is a solid?
list.why: Clay is a solid.

list.q: Which of these is a liquid?
list.why: Water is a liquid.

list.q: Which of these is a liquid?
list.why: Oil flows and takes the shape of its container.

list.q: Which of these is a liquid?
list.why: Syrup pours — it's a liquid.

list.q: Which of these is a gas?
list.why: Air is a gas: it has no shape and fills the balloon.

list.q: Which of these is a gas?
list.why: Helium is a gas.

list.q: A balloon is blown up. The air inside…
list.a: spreads out to fill the whole balloon
w: stays at the bottom like water
list.why: Gases fill the container they are in.

list.q: You pour juice from a tall glass into a wide bowl. What happens to the juice's shape?
list.a: It takes the shape of the bowl
list.why: Liquids take the shape of their containers.

list.q: You move a block from a box to a bag. What happens to the block's shape?
list.why: Solids keep their own shape.

list.q: Name one solid, one liquid and one gas we use every day.
list.why: Many everyday examples: a solid (wood), a liquid (water), a gas (air).

list.q: Which clue tells you something is a liquid?
list.a: It pours and takes the shape of its container
list.why: Liquids flow.

list.q: Which clue tells you something is a solid?
w: It spreads out to fill a room
list.why: Solids keep their shape.

list.q: A toy needs a raincoat. Which material is best for keeping water out?
list.why: Foil is best for blocking water because it stayed dry.
list.hint: Think: which one stayed dry when water was dropped on it?

list.q: Which material is best for cleaning up a spill?
list.why: A sponge is absorbent — it soaks up water.

list.q: What does “absorbent” mean?
list.why: Absorbency is how well something soaks up water.

list.q: What does “water resistant” mean?
list.why: Water-resistant materials block water.

list.q: What does “flexible” mean?
list.why: Flexibility is how easily something bends.

list.q: In the strength test, what do you check?
list.a: Whether the material can hold a block
list.why: Strength: can it hold a block?

list.q: Which is the best way to choose a material for a job?
list.why: We match materials to the best job using evidence from tests.

list.q: Which material is good for holding something heavy?
list.a: cardboard that passed the strength test
list.why: A strong material that held a block is best for heavy jobs.

list.q: Why is foil a good choice to block water?
list.a: It stayed dry when water was dropped on it
list.why: Evidence: foil stayed dry.

list.q: Ice melts and then is refrozen. Can it change back?
list.why: Melting and refreezing ice is reversible.

list.q: Chocolate melts and then cools. Can it change back?
list.why: Melted chocolate becomes solid again when it cools.

list.q: Bread is toasted. Can it change back?
list.why: Toasting (cooking) bread changes it for good.

list.q: Playdough is squished into a new shape. Can it change back?
list.why: Playdough can be reshaped back.

list.q: What does “reversible” mean?
list.why: A reversible change can be undone.

list.q: What does “irreversible” mean?
list.why: Irreversible changes can't be undone.

list.q: Which is an irreversible change?
list.why: Cooking changes food for good.

list.q: Heating can change matter. What happens when you heat ice?
list.why: Heat melts ice into water.

list.q: What happens when you cool water until it is very cold?
list.why: Cooling water makes ice — a solid.

list.q: Name the five ways matter can change that the class sorted.
list.a: Melting, freezing, cooking, breaking and mixing
list.why: Melting, freezing, cooking, breaking, mixing.

list.q: Which change is freezing?
list.why: Freezing: liquid → solid.

list.q: Which change is melting?
list.why: Melting: solid → liquid.

list.q: What is oobleck made from?
list.why: Mix about 1½ cups of cornstarch with 1¼ cups of water.

list.q: A non-Newtonian fluid is a mixture that…
list.a: acts like both a liquid and a solid
list.why: It has parts of both a liquid and a solid.

list.q: What happens if you press oobleck slowly with your fingers?
list.a: Your fingers sink in like a liquid
list.why: Slow, gentle pressure → it acts like a liquid.

list.q: What happens if you punch oobleck quickly and hard?
list.why: Fast, hard force → it acts like a solid.

list.q: What happens when you press two fingers into water and then punch it?
list.a: Your fingers go in and it splashes — it stays a liquid
list.why: Water is a plain liquid; it doesn't turn solid.

list.q: What happens when you punch a solid tabletop?
list.a: It stays hard and does not give
list.why: A solid keeps its shape.

list.q: If you run across a river of quicksand, it will act like a…
list.why: Moving fast makes it act like a solid.

list.q: If you slowly step into quicksand, it will act like a…
list.why: Moving slowly, it acts like a liquid.

list.q: Why is oobleck special?
list.a: It can act like a liquid AND a solid
w: It only comes from the ocean
list.why: Oobleck is a non-Newtonian fluid.

list.q: Which two ingredients make a non-Newtonian fluid in the experiment?
list.why: Cornstarch + water.

list.q: In the oobleck experiment, what do you do to make it difficult to stir but not too dry?
list.a: Mix cornstarch and water, adding a bit more of either if needed
list.why: Adjust the cornstarch and water until it is the right consistency.
